strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets and 8 diverse task families (fine-grained understanding, bounding box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image-text retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction, LMM integration, ablations), with consistent gains over strong recent baselines (SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, MetaCLIP 2) across nearly all settings and multiple backbone scales (Base/Large/So400M).

Fills a genuine and previously underserved gap: unifying fine-grained (region-level) alignment with bilingual (English-Chinese) capability in a single dual-encoder framework, whereas prior work addressed these axes separately.

Contributes a new and useful set of Chinese evaluation resources (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN for long-caption retrieval; BoxClass-CN for region-level classification) that address a real scarcity of fine-grained Chinese multimodal benchmarks, with reasonably detailed construction pipelines and category schema provided in the appendix.

The proposed TIC loss and CMR loss with global threshold synchronization are reasonably well-motivated and ablations (Table 7) show meaningful, non-trivial contributions to hard-negative discrimination (FG-OVD Hard, COCO Top-1), lending some support to the specific technical contributions beyond just data/scale.

Demonstrates downstream transfer value: gains carry over to open-vocabulary detection (via fused confidence with LLMDet), dense prediction (Cat-Seg), and as a vision encoder in LLaVA-style LMMs, suggesting practical utility beyond intrinsic alignment metrics.
Plans to release model, code, and benchmark, supporting reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: Most individual components (sigmoid/SigLIP loss, RoIAlign region alignment, hard-negative textual discrimination à la FG-CLIP, rank/margin loss adapted from Zhang et al. 2024b) are incremental adaptations of existing techniques; the main technical novelty is largely confined to the TIC loss and the global-threshold synchronization for CMR, which are relatively modest contributions relative to the paper's scale of claims.

Much of the reported superiority likely stems from substantially larger and more heavily curated/re-captioned training data (1.6B enhanced LAION captions, 500M in-house Chinese pairs, in-house Chinese region data) rather than the proposed architectural/loss innovations; without data-matched baselines or an ablation isolating the effect of data scale/curation vs. objectives, it is hard to attribute gains to the claimed methodological contributions.

The new Chinese benchmarks are constructed via automated LMM-based pipelines (captioning, translation, detection, similarity filtering) with limited independent quality control beyond brief mention of native-speaker validation for translations only; BoxClass-CN's category set (566 classes derived via clustering/merging with a 0.15 similarity threshold from FG-CLIP itself) risks circularity since FG-CLIP-family models are also evaluated on it and FG-CLIP was used to construct the very filtering criterion.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance analysis are reported despite fine-grained differences between methods sometimes being small (e.g., ImageNet-1K/v2, some retrieval numbers), making it difficult to assess robustness of the comparisons.

Some baseline comparisons appear incomplete or inconsistent across backbone families (e.g., missing FineCLIP/CLIPSelf entries for larger backbones, inconsistent ViT-L/14 vs ViT-L/16 designations across tables), and it is unclear whether all baselines were re-evaluated under identical protocols or taken from original papers, raising reproducibility concerns for exact numbers.

Fixed loss weights (λ1–λ5) are stated as chosen for 'stable and effective' training without ablation or sensitivity analysis, and hyperparameter choices such as the 0.95 similarity filter and top-10 hard negative selection for TIC are not justified empirically.

The paper does not discuss computational cost/resource footprint (e.g., 160 NPUs + 16 H800 GPUs for training) in terms of accessibility/reproducibility for the broader research community, nor provide wall-clock/carbon cost estimates.

Limitations section is very brief and mostly forward-looking (longer inputs, relational structures) rather than critically engaging with the identified weaknesses above (e.g., data-scale confounds, benchmark circularity, or potential biases introduced by LMM-generated captions).

strengths: The paper conducts an unusually broad empirical evaluation (29 datasets, 8 task families: fine-grained region discrimination, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image/long-caption retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction/segmentation, and LMM integration), which gives a fairly comprehensive picture of the model's behavior across scales (Base/Large/So400M).

The introduction of Chinese fine-grained evaluation resources (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN for long-caption retrieval, and BoxClass-CN for region-level classification) addresses a genuine and previously under-served gap, since most existing Chinese multimodal benchmarks are limited to short-caption retrieval.

The ablation in Table 7 cleanly isolates the contribution of the two newly combined objectives (L_CMR and L_TIC), showing non-trivial degradation when each is removed, which supports the internal consistency of the design choices.

Consistent, often sizable improvements over strong recent baselines (SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, MetaCLIP 2, Chinese-CLIP, R2D2) across nearly every reported benchmark and model scale, including with a smaller backbone than MetaCLIP 2's ViT-H/14, suggests practical utility of the released model.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: the architecture is a direct extension of SigLIP 2, the fine-grained textual objective and hard-negative construction are taken essentially unchanged from FG-CLIP/FineHARD, and the CMR loss is adopted from Zhang et al. (2024b) with only a global-threshold-synchronization engineering tweak that is not separately ablated. The TIC loss is a fairly standard intra-modal contrastive formulation. The paper reads more as a large-scale engineering/system report than as a paper advancing new modeling ideas.

Reproducibility is substantially undermined by heavy reliance on proprietary, non-released data: 500M in-house Chinese image-text pairs and 12M in-house Chinese region-text pairs constitute a large fraction of training data, yet only the model/benchmark/code are promised, not this core data. Given the scale of compute used (160 Ascend 910B NPUs + 16 H800 GPUs), independent verification or ablation by other groups is effectively infeasible.

Because gains likely stem from a confound of (a) much larger/curated proprietary training corpora, (b) a stronger pretrained SigLIP2 backbone, and (c) the proposed losses, the paper does not isolate how much of the improvement is attributable to the claimed methodological contributions (TIC, CMR synchronization) versus simply more/better data at larger scale. No controlled comparison trains baselines on the same data mixture.

The automatically constructed benchmarks (BoxClass-CN via detector + LMM captioning + NMS + similarity filtering with FG-CLIP itself; LIT-CN captions generated by an LMM) raise circularity and quality concerns — using FG-CLIP's own similarity scores to filter BoxClass-CN region-text pairs could bias the benchmark toward favoring FG-CLIP-family models. Validation by native speakers is reported only for DCI-CN/DOCCI-CN translations, not for LIT-CN or the BoxClass-CN category translations.

No variance/robustness reporting (single-run numbers throughout, no confidence intervals or multiple seeds), and no discussion of compute cost, environmental impact, or data licensing/ethics for the large-scale web-crawled and in-house datasets, despite the very large training budget.

The limitations section is extremely brief and generic (extending text length, modeling object relations) and does not engage with the more material limitations above (data opacity, benchmark circularity, confounded ablations, compute reproducibility barrier for the broader community).

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets and 8 task families (fine-grained region-text discrimination, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, short/long-caption retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense segmentation, and downstream LMM integration), giving a convincing multi-angle picture of the model's capabilities in both English and Chinese.

Fills a genuine gap by unifying fine-grained (region-level) alignment and bilingual (English-Chinese) support in a single framework, whereas prior works (FineCLIP, FG-CLIP vs. Chinese-CLIP/R2D2) address these axes separately.

Contributes new Chinese evaluation resources (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN for long-caption retrieval, and BoxClass-CN for region-level classification) that address a real scarcity of fine-grained Chinese multimodal benchmarks and could be useful to the community independent of the model itself.

The proposed Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss and the Cross-modal Rank loss with global threshold synchronization are reasonably motivated, and the ablation study (Table 7) demonstrates their individual and combined contributions, including a sizable 4.8-point COCO Top-1 drop when TIC is removed.

Consistent, often large margins over strong, recent baselines (SigLIP2, Meta CLIP2, FG-CLIP, FineCLIP, Long-CLIP) across backbone scales (Base/Large/So400M), and the model remains competitive on standard zero-shot classification, indicating fine-grained gains do not come at the cost of global recognition.

Demonstrated downstream utility beyond pure alignment metrics: improvements transfer to open-vocabulary detection (with LLMDet), dense segmentation (with Cat-Seg), and as a vision encoder in an LLaVA-style LMM, strengthening the practical significance of the contribution.
Commitment to release model, code, and benchmark aids future reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: Substantial reliance on large-scale in-house, non-public data (500M Chinese image-text pairs, 12M Chinese region-text pairs, plus an 'enhanced' LAION-2B with LMM-generated long captions) makes full reproduction of training impossible for external researchers even with code/model release; the paper does not clarify whether these in-house datasets will also be released.

The BoxClass-CN benchmark construction pipeline uses FG-CLIP itself (a closely related prior model from the same lineage) to filter region-text pairs by similarity threshold (>0.15), which risks a methodological circularity that could bias the benchmark toward favoring FG-CLIP-family models over unrelated baselines.

The ablation study is incomplete: it only isolates L_CMR and L_TIC against a baseline that already includes global, fine-grained visual, and fine-grained textual losses, but never shows the independent contribution of L_FGV or L_FGT, nor justifies the fixed loss weights (λ1–λ5) via sensitivity analysis.

No variance/error bars or repeated-run statistics are reported for any benchmark, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (sometimes only 0.1–1 point, e.g., ImageNet-1K Top-1 vs. SigLIP2) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

Comparisons across model families are not fully controlled for training data scale/composition (e.g., FG-CLIP 2 vs. Meta CLIP 2 differ in both parameter count and training corpora), so performance differences cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed architecture/losses versus data scale or curation differences.

DCI-CN and DOCCI-CN are produced via LMM translation of English captions (with only native-speaker validation, not independent authoring), which may embed translation artifacts or English-centric phrasing patterns rather than naturally Chinese descriptive style, somewhat limiting their value as a purely 'Chinese' fine-grained benchmark.

The architectural contribution is incremental (built directly on SigLIP2 plus FG-CLIP's hard-negative/region-text recipe extended to two languages and two stages), so the core novelty rests mainly on the TIC loss, data curation, and new benchmarks rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach.

Limited discussion of failure modes, computational cost (e.g., total GPU/NPU-hours, which appear very large: 160 Ascend 910B + 16 H800 nodes), or limitations beyond a brief forward-looking statement about longer text and relational modeling.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets across 8 diverse task families (fine-grained region classification, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image-text retrieval at both short and long caption lengths, zero-shot classification, dense/segmentation prediction, and downstream LMM integration), giving strong evidence that the gains are not confined to a narrow benchmark.

Fills a genuine and previously underserved gap by releasing a suite of Chinese fine-grained evaluation benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) and a new 12M-image Chinese region-text training corpus (FineRegion-CN), which should be broadly useful to the community.

Reasonably careful ablations: loss-component ablation (TIC, CMR) showing meaningful drops when removed, a controlled bilingual-vs-English-only data ablation isolating the mutual benefit of bilingual training, and a re-trained-baseline comparison (Appendix E) that controls for training data to isolate architectural/objective contributions from data effects.

Consistent and often large improvements over strong, recent, comparably-sized baselines (SigLIP 2, MetaCLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP) across nearly all reported tasks and backbone scales, and demonstrated transfer benefit when used as a vision encoder in a full LMM (LLaVA-1.5) and as a scorer for open-vocabulary detection, indicating practical downstream utility beyond retrieval metrics alone.

Good transparency in the appendix: detailed hyperparameter tuning procedure, dataset composition tables, qualitative visualizations (dense feature alignment maps, TIC embedding separability), and example captions/categories, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overall technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework largely composes existing ingredients (SigLIP2 backbone, FG-CLIP-style hard-negative fine-grained textual/visual losses, dual short/long caption training as in Long-CLIP-style works, CMR loss from prior work). The main new component, the TIC loss, is a fairly straightforward intra-modal hard-negative contrastive objective and its marginal benefit, while nontrivial, is modest relative to the paper's other engineering contributions.

Potential circularity in the BoxClass-CN benchmark construction: region-text pairs are filtered using region-text similarity computed by FG-CLIP (a prior version of the authors' own model family) with a threshold of 0.15, which could bias the resulting benchmark toward pairs that FG-CLIP-family models are already predisposed to score well on, weakening the objectivity of FG-CLIP 2's strong results on this specific benchmark.

The Chinese long-caption benchmarks (DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN) are produced by machine-translating English captions with an LMM and validating with native speakers, but details of the validation protocol (number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, error rates) are not reported, leaving open questions about benchmark quality and translation artifacts.

No variance/multiple-run reporting or statistical significance testing is provided anywhere in the paper; given that many performance gaps over the strongest baselines (e.g., SigLIP 2, Meta CLIP 2) are sometimes small in specific settings (e.g., ImageNet-1K/v2 classification, some VOC/PC segmentation numbers), it is hard to assess whether improvements are robust.

Loss weights (λ1–λ4) are tuned via a sequential greedy search directly against validation performance on the same task families used for final evaluation, raising some concern about overfitting the training recipe to the reported benchmarks rather than a more principled or held-out selection procedure.

The Impact Statement is essentially a non-statement ("none which we feel must be specifically highlighted") despite the paper training on hundreds of millions of web-scraped image-text pairs (LAION, Wukong, in-house 500M Chinese data) and releasing large new datasets; potential privacy, bias, and content-moderation issues in the released Chinese region-text and web-derived benchmark data are not discussed.

Backbone comparisons are not always strictly matched (e.g., ViT-L/14 vs ViT-L/16, or comparing FG-CLIP 2 ViT-So/16 against MetaCLIP 2 ViT-H/14 with far more parameters), which the paper acknowledges positively as an efficiency argument but which also complicates precise attribution of gains to the proposed method versus backbone/resolution differences.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets and 8 task families (fine-grained discrimination, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction, and LMM integration), which is a substantial engineering effort.

Release of a new large-scale Chinese region-text dataset (FineRegion-CN, 12M images) and a new Chinese fine-grained evaluation suite (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN), addressing a genuine gap in non-English fine-grained VL benchmarking.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (loss components, bilingual vs. English-only data, retrained baselines under matched data) that attempt to isolate the sources of improvement.
Consistent, sizeable quantitative gains over many open-source baselines across the reported benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the architecture is SigLIP2 with only incremental modifications (longer text length, data-adaptive resolution, RoI-based region head), the global loss is the existing sigmoid loss, and the Cross-modal Rank loss is adopted essentially verbatim from Zhang et al. (2024b); the main claimed novelty (TIC loss) is a fairly standard intra-modal hard-negative contrastive objective and its presented formula (Eq. 1) lacks a clear positive-pair term, making the described objective hard to verify as written.

The work reads largely as a data-scaling and engineering exercise (massive proprietary in-house Chinese corpus of 500M pairs, 160 Ascend NPUs + 16 H800 GPUs) rather than a methodological advance, limiting reproducibility for most of the community despite the stated code/model release.

Comparisons are sometimes not strictly controlled: FG-CLIP 2 is compared against competitor backbones of different parameter counts/patch sizes (e.g., ViT-L/16 vs ViT-L/14, ViT-So/16 vs ViT-H/14), which confounds architecture, scale, and training-recipe effects and makes 'state-of-the-art' claims less clean.

No reported variance/multiple-run statistics anywhere; single-run numbers are used to claim significance of gains, including in ablations where differences are sometimes small (e.g., CMR removal changes trivial FG-OVD accuracy by only ~1.5 points in the direction opposite to other metrics).

New benchmark construction relies heavily on LMM-generated captions and translations with only vague validation ('validated by native speakers' with no details on number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, or error rates), and object categories/boxes are produced by automatic detectors and similarity thresholds (FG-CLIP itself), raising circularity/bias concerns given FG-CLIP's descendant model is evaluated on this benchmark.

The Limitations and Impact Statement sections are extremely superficial (a single forward-looking sentence and a boilerplate statement claiming no notable societal risks), despite the work using large web-scraped, LMM-captioned corpora (LAION, Wukong, in-house 500M) that plausibly carry licensing, privacy, and content-safety concerns which are not discussed.

Fixed loss weights are selected via a greedy sequential tuning heuristic without reporting sensitivity ranges beyond a narrow hyperparameter sweep on one representative subset of tasks/backbone, leaving open how robust the chosen weights are across scales and languages.

Some result tables contain missing baseline entries (e.g., FineCLIP missing MSCOCO/Flickr30k numbers for ViT-L, CLOC missing many columns), reducing completeness and making some superiority claims only partially substantiated.

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets and 8 task families (fine-grained region/text discrimination, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image-level retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction/segmentation, and downstream LMM integration), across three backbone scales (ViT-B/L/So). This breadth gives strong evidence that the gains are not an artifact of a single benchmark or task type.

Fills a genuine and underexplored gap: bilingual (Chinese-English) fine-grained vision-language alignment. Most prior fine-grained CLIP variants (FineCLIP, LongCLIP, FG-CLIP) are English-only, and prior Chinese models (Chinese-CLIP, R2D2) are coarse-grained; this paper unifies both axes in one framework.

Valuable new resources released to the community: a 12M-image Chinese region-text dataset (FineRegion-CN) and a suite of Chinese fine-grained evaluation benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN), addressing a clear shortage of rigorous Chinese multimodal benchmarks beyond short-caption retrieval.

The proposed Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss is simple, well-motivated, and shown to meaningfully improve fine-grained discrimination (e.g., 4.8-point COCO Top-1 drop when removed), with qualitative similarity-matrix visualizations (Appendix H) supporting the claimed mechanism of improved intra-modal separability.

Careful controlled ablations that help isolate sources of improvement: a bilingual vs. English-only Stage-II data ablation (Appendix D) and, notably, a re-trained-baseline comparison (SigLIP2, Chinese-CLIP retrained on identical Stage-II data, Appendix E) that helps disentangle the contribution of architecture/objectives from training data advantages — a control that is often missing in similar papers.

Demonstrated transfer value beyond intrinsic alignment metrics: integration into LLaVA-style LMMs and into an open-vocabulary detector (LLMDet) shows consistent downstream gains, supporting the practical significance of the proposed representations.
weaknesses: Substantial reliance on a large (500M-pair) proprietary in-house Chinese dataset whose curation process is not described, which limits reproducibility of the full training pipeline even though code/model/benchmark are promised to be released.

The construction of the Chinese benchmarks relies heavily on the same class of LMMs used elsewhere in the pipeline (Qwen2.5-VL for captioning/translation), with validation described only briefly as checked by "native speakers" — no details on number of annotators, agreement rates, or sampling for quality control, raising some concern about annotation rigor and potential systematic translation artifacts.

BoxClass-CN construction filters region-text pairs using similarity scores computed by FG-CLIP (the predecessor of the proposed model's family) at a fixed threshold; using a closely related model to build an evaluation benchmark risks a mild circularity/selection bias favoring the FG-CLIP lineage, which is not discussed as a limitation.

All reported results appear to be single-run numbers with no variance/error bars or statistical significance testing, which is a common but non-trivial limitation given many margins between methods are a few points.

Design choices in TIC and CMR losses (e.g., 0.95 similarity filter threshold, top-10 hard negatives, fixed loss weights found via sequential/greedy tuning) are justified empirically but lack deeper analysis of sensitivity or theoretical grounding; the hyperparameter ablation in Appendix F sweeps one dimension at a time rather than jointly, which may miss interaction effects.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with issues specific to this work, such as the use of large-scale uncurated web/LAION data (potential licensing, privacy, or representational bias concerns), or implications of releasing a 12M-image Chinese region-text dataset.

Some sections (e.g., architecture description, resolution strategy) are described somewhat tersely without ablating individual design choices (e.g., contribution of the data-adaptive resolution strategy itself vs. SigLIP2's stochastic sampling) in isolation.
